analysis.title: Monthly Market Review, October 2026
key_insights: Q3 2026 GDP preliminary reading was +3.4% QoQ annualized, in line with Raymond James expectations. Private investment rose 19.4% on the AI buildout and consumer spending rose 3.8%, led by services.

Tensions between the US and Iran stayed elevated. The US continues to blockade the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi strikes on Saudi refineries pushed crude back above $100/bbl. Gas prices are above $4/gallon.

The Fed held rates at 3.75%-4.00% in October with a hawkish tone. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a 25bp hike. Chairman Warsh said the committee needs to accumulate more information and cited geopolitical uncertainty.
Market pricing for Fed hikes over the next 12 months fell to two from four a month earlier.
September headline CPI was +3.7% YoY, the fastest pace since May, with about 50% of the increase attributed to fuel prices. Core CPI was +2.6% YoY against +2.5% expected.
September payrolls added only 29k jobs and unemployment rose to 4.2% from 4.1%. Initial jobless claims (~194k) have been at or below 200k for 7 straight weeks, the longest streak since 1969.
Consumer Confidence rose 7.5 points to 91.7, the fastest monthly rise since May 2025. Consumers plan to spend less on services and durable goods over the next six months because of sticky inflation.

Retail Sales headline rose 0.8% MoM on higher gas prices, while the Control Group rose only 0.1%. Housing data was soft apart from existing home sales, and the 30-year mortgage rate reached about 7.5%, the highest since April 2024.

Treasuries (+2.4% MoM) had their best month since December 2023 as the 2-, 10- and 30-year yields each fell about 30bps. The Bloomberg US Aggregate also gained 2.4%. The report attributes the move to fears of reduced AI investment.
Credit spreads widened. IG spreads rose about 10bps to about 90bps, HY about 28bps to about 340bps (CCC +110bps), and EM about 26bps to about 196bps.
Municipals returned +3.9% in October, their best October since at least 1980 after the worst month since 2008.
A global tech-led selloff hit EM Asia and the US hardest. MSCI EM fell 8.0%, MSCI Asia ex Japan 8.2%, and MSCI AC World 1.6%. EM underperformed EAFE by the widest margin since October 2022.

The S&P 500 fell 0.9% while nine of 11 sectors rose. Energy (+14.0%) and Consumer Staples (+11.6%) led, while Communication Services (-15.1%) and Tech (-6.8%) lagged. Large-cap value beat large-cap growth by the widest margin since February 2001. Russell 1000 Growth fell 6.1% against Russell 1000 Value +4.4%.
The Russell 2000 gained 0.6% and outperformed large caps for the first time in four months as falling yields helped small caps.

Crude oil (WTI) rose 15.2% and ended above $100/bbl for the first time since April. Gold fell 6.9% to below $4,000/oz for the first time since October 2025 and silver fell 18.6%. The Bloomberg Grains Index fell 9.1%.
The US Dollar Index rose 0.4% for a second straight month to its highest level since April 2025, supported by US growth and Fed hawkishness.

China manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 (contraction) and Euro Zone manufacturing PMI eased to 52.4. ISM Manufacturing was 55.5, the tenth straight month in expansion, with production at the fastest pace since November 2021.

Rates were held with two dissents in favor of a 25bp hike. The tone was hawkish and Chairman Warsh wants more information before deciding policy.

Weak job creation, while unemployment rose to 4.2% from 4.1%.

Driven mainly by higher gas prices, not broader demand.
Eased considerably, which signals softer underlying consumer demand.

Contraction on weaker overseas orders and softer consumer demand after the National Day Holiday.

risk_factors: AI demand and financing concerns could reduce AI investment and keep pressuring tech.
Sticky inflation, with fuel prices and core CPI both elevated, erodes consumer purchasing power.
Continued US/Iran conflict and the Hormuz blockade keep oil above $100/bbl.
Credit spreads are widening at the lower end of credit quality, with CCC spreads up 110bps.
A weaker labor market, with only 29k jobs added in September and unemployment up to 4.2%.
A stronger US dollar and high mortgage rates (~7.5%) weigh on housing and global growth.
Weak Chinese demand and softening global manufacturing.

The US continues to blockade the Strait of Hormuz.

Global supply constraints from the US/Iran conflict support crude oil prices.

tension_points.bull_case: Q3 GDP was supported by a 19.4% rise in private investment from the AI buildout, and ISM production grew at the fastest pace since November 2021.
tension_points.bear_case: Fears of reduced AI investment and AI demand/financing concerns drove tech weakness, with Tech -6.8% and Comm. Services -15.1% in October.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI demand and financing concerns drove tech weakness and Treasury yields lower, even as AI buildout supported GDP.
theme_stances.evidence: AI demand/financing concerns drove tech weakness.

theme_stances.key_argument: Supply constraints from the US/Iran conflict pushed crude above $100/bbl and boosted energy.
theme_stances.evidence: Crude oil ended the month above $100/bbl for the first time since April
